profile.name: Hai Nguyen
profile.about:
Five years across corporate finance, start-up strategy and venture investing in Southeast Asia. I'm an Investment Associate at Openspace Capital, a multi-stage venture fund with US$800M under management, where I led Every Half Coffee's US$8M Series A.

Before that I co-led Rize's US$31M Series B, structured a US$11M debt facility for smallholder rice farmers and closed the company's first carbon credit offtake. At Shopee I built the models and forecasts behind senior leadership's investment decisions.

Outside deal work, I build tools that answer questions I keep running into as an investor, using only public data. I set the question, the rules and the standard of evidence; Claude writes the code, and everything runs on a free stack of GitHub Actions and Cloudflare. Each number traces back to a public source, nothing uses information that wasn't available at the time, and a rule stays only if the data supports it.
profile.motto: Wharton economics. English, Vietnamese and Mandarin.

projects.title: Carbon Credit Atlas
projects.summary: A free map of carbon credit projects across every major registry, with who is buying them.
projects.context: Carbon credit data is split across more than ten registries and programmes — Verra, Gold Standard, the UN's CDM, Global Carbon Council, UCR, Japan's JCM, Puro.earth, Isometric and Paris Agreement Article 6 — each with its own format. Buyers are mostly named only in press releases. Working on Rize's first carbon credit offtake, I had no single place to see which projects exist in a market, how much they have issued and who buys them.
projects.objective: One public, verifiable view of every project in a region: where it is, its credit type, stage and volumes, and its announced buyers. It started with Asia excluding mainland China and now covers every region.
methodology: One collector per registry or programme. Each checks a cheap change signal first and downloads only what changed, on a schedule.
Records are normalised to one schema: country codes, a two-level credit-type taxonomy and project stages (listed, validated, issuing).
Projects listed in more than one registry are merged by fuzzy name matching, with hard checks on capacity, place and technology; borderline pairs go to a review queue.
Buyers come only from public announcements and registry retirement records, each with its source link. Nothing is inferred.
Every row links back to its registry record. An independent review of 300 random projects put keyword-tag precision at about 98%.
Runs at no cost: GitHub Actions collects the data and Cloudflare hosts the site.

projects.title: Biotech Crash Triage
projects.summary: Calls each US biotech stock that has just crashed a Buy candidate, Watch or Avoid, and backtests every call.
projects.context: When a biotech stock halves on trial news, specialist investors say some falls are deserved and some are not, but that judgement is tacit and rarely tested. Average post-crash returns hide the difference between a company with cash, committed funds and other programmes, and one about to raise money on harsh terms.
projects.objective: On the day a crash or slide is detected, give a rule-based call using only data that was public that day, and check every past call against what happened over the following year.
methodology: Universe: every SEC pharma and biotech filer since 2021 (about 1,040 companies), including those later acquired or delisted, so there is no survivorship bias.
Two triggers: a crash (down 50% within 5 trading days, with a 25% news day) and a slide (30% below the 6-month high, with no 25% single-day fall).

Inputs from primary sources: SEC balance sheets, insider trades (Form 4), fund holdings (13F), offering documents, short interest and ClinicalTrials.gov. Claude reads each crash announcement, and every fact is checked against a verbatim quote.
No look-ahead: each input counts only from its public filing date, and an episode with incomplete inputs gets no call.

A rule is kept only if it holds in both halves of the history, in every entry year and under a company-clustered bootstrap. After July 2023, crash Buy candidates failed 46% of the time against 82% for Watch.
Returns are compared with the 10 most similar biotechs and the XBI index, and a public ledger timestamps each new call.

projects.title: Macro Compass
projects.summary: Reads 28 public US signals to say where the economy, inflation and markets stand.
projects.context: Macro calls are often made from a few remembered thresholds and anecdotes: one yield level, one indicator, one company's comments. The reading is rarely checked against history, and noisy monthly data makes it easy to change your mind too often.
projects.objective: One page that answers three questions — is the economy weakening, is inflation running hot, are markets under stress — and shows the evidence behind each answer.
methodology: 28 signals in three groups: 13 on the economy (the Sahm rule, the yield curve, truck tonnage, building permits, vehicle sales, sector leadership), 7 on inflation and 8 on market stress (VIX, credit spreads, the dollar, semiconductors).
Each signal has a warning zone set from its own history, shown on a long-run chart with US recessions shaded, plus whether it is better or worse than a year ago.
Each group's reading uses 6-month averages, and the economy reading changes only after 3 months in a row, so one noisy print can't flip it.
The three readings combine into an overall phase of the cycle, such as Recovery, with a plain-English line for every signal.
